tagline: Heat, redness, swelling, pain: the body's alarm and its first step toward healing.
overview: Inflammation is the body's complex, nonspecific response to injury, infection, or harmful agents. It walls off damage, clears debris, and starts repair, but it can become harmful: overactive mediators cause allergic reactions and anaphylaxis, and inflammation that will not switch off drives chronic and autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis. Nurses spot inflammation early, tell local findings from systemic ones, give anti-inflammatory drugs safely, and support healing across the lifespan.

topics.title: What Inflammation Is (and Isn't)
topics.summary: A complex, nonspecific, protective response to harm that promotes healing, but can become harmful when it is misdirected or will not switch off.

sections.heading: Definition and purpose
sections.body: Inflammation is a complex, nonspecific bodily response to harm. It is a protective mechanism that promotes healing and prevents further damage. It is an adaptive, nonspecific immune response that brings fluid, substances, and blood cells to the injury site. Its goals are to neutralize the invader, clear damaged tissue, and begin repair.
bullets: Inflammation is not the same as infection. Infection means microorganisms have invaded. Inflammation is the body's response, and it can happen with no microbes at all (a sprain, a burn, a sunburn).
Disorders that involve the inflammatory process end in -itis: bronchitis, colitis, gastritis, appendicitis, nephritis, pancreatitis, dermatitis, cholecystitis.
Inflammation can become harmful and lead to autoimmune disease: rheumatoid arthritis (RA), systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), psoriasis, and Guillain-Barré syndrome.

sections.heading: Causes (triggers)
sections.body: Inflammation is triggered by injury, infection, or harmful agents.
bullets: Microorganisms: bacteria, fungi, viruses, parasites
Chemical agents: internal acids (e.g., gastric acid) and external poisons
Physical agents: trauma, heat or cold, radiation (including sunburn)

sections.heading: Healthy response, local vs. generalized
sections.body: A healthy response activates and recruits white blood cells (WBCs) to the site. Localized inflammation stays at a specific site and shows the classic signs (redness, heat, swelling, pain, impaired function). Generalized inflammation produces systemic effects: fever, a rising heart rate and respiratory rate, a rising WBC count or bands, fatigue, and loss of appetite.
bullets: Chronic inflammation example from the slides: rheumatoid arthritis, in which ongoing joint inflammation leads to deformity.
Overactivation of the inflammatory mediators causes allergic reactions and anaphylaxis.

pearls: On NCLEX, '-itis' plus fever and a rising WBC count means inflammation, possibly with infection. Ask whether the process is still local or has become systemic.
A client can be inflamed without being infected. A red, warm, swollen ankle after a sprain does not need an antibiotic.
redFlags: Local signs that spread (red streaking, expanding redness) or systemic signs (high fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, rising WBC or bands) mean the process is no longer contained. Notify the provider.

topics.title: The 5 Classic (Cardinal) Signs
topics.summary: Redness, heat, swelling, pain, and impaired (loss of) function, each explained by what the blood vessels and mediators are doing.

sections.heading: Why each sign happens
sections.body: The classic signs are the vascular response made visible. If you know the mechanism, you can predict which intervention helps. For example, elevation and ice reduce swelling because they lower hydrostatic pressure and blood flow to the site.

table.caption: Cardinal signs of inflammation
rows: Vasodilation → ↑ blood flow to the area (histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins)
Outline the edges of redness to track spread
↑ blood flow to the site; prostaglandins also cause systemic fever
Compare the site with the same area on the other side using the back of the hand; monitor temperature
↑ capillary permeability → fluid and proteins leak into the tissue (exudate)
Elevate, apply ice early, check circulation distal to the swelling
Bradykinin and prostaglandins stimulate nerve endings; pressure from edema
Assess with a pain scale; NSAIDs block prostaglandins
Rest and position in the acute phase; restore activity as cleared (physical therapy)

pearls: Swelling in a small space can be dangerous: swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat can block the airway.
After applying ice or a wrap, always check circulation, movement, and sensation distal to it.
redFlags: Pale, cool, numb, or tingling skin, or delayed capillary refill distal to swelling or a wrap means circulation is impaired. Loosen the wrap and notify the provider.
Swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, hoarseness, or stridor suggests anaphylaxis. The airway is the priority.

topics.title: Stages of Inflammation
topics.summary: Stage 1: vascular and cellular response. Stage 2: exudate production. Stage 3: repair by regeneration or scar.

sections.heading: Stage 1: Vascular and cellular response
sections.body: Right after injury there is a brief arteriolar vasoconstriction lasting seconds. It is quickly followed by vasodilation (more blood to the area → redness and heat). Mediators such as histamine increase capillary permeability, so fluid and proteins leak into the tissue (swelling). Blood flow slows, and WBCs move to the vessel wall.
bullets: Margination: WBCs line up along the vessel wall
Adhesion: they stick to the vessel wall
Emigration (diapedesis): they squeeze out through the vessel wall
Chemotaxis: they follow chemical signals toward the injury
Phagocytosis: they engulf and destroy microbes and debris
Neutrophils arrive first and are the main cell in pus. Monocytes follow and become macrophages, which clean up and signal repair.
The bone marrow releases more neutrophils, including immature bands, so the WBC count and bands rise (a left shift).

sections.heading: Stage 2: Exudate production
sections.body: Exudate is the fluid, cells, and proteins that leak from the vessels at the site. It dilutes toxins, carries WBCs to the area, and helps wall off the injury. Its type and trend tell you what is happening in the wound.

sections.heading: Stage 3: Reparative phase
sections.body: The process shifts from inflammation to repair. Regeneration replaces damaged cells with identical or similar cells. When regeneration is not possible, the tissue heals by scar formation.
bullets: Quick regeneration: skin, GI and respiratory tract lining, bone, bone marrow, lymphoid tissue
Limited regeneration: nervous tissue, muscle (including heart muscle), elastic tissue. These heal by scar.
Granulation tissue: fragile, red or pink, moist, with many new capillaries. It bleeds easily and is a sign of healthy healing.
Cicatrix (scar tissue): firm, fibrous, and less functional than the tissue it replaces.
Repair needs adequate fluids, protein, carbohydrates, and vitamins, especially vitamin C.

table.caption: Types of exudate
rows: Early inflammation, blisters; small amounts are expected
Expected on fresh surgical incisions; should decrease and lighten

Infection: WBCs, dead tissue, and microbes

pearls: Serosanguineous drainage that becomes less and paler over time is expected. Drainage that becomes purulent or suddenly bright red is not.
Red or pink, moist granulation tissue is good. Pale, gray, or friable tissue suggests poor healing or infection.
redFlags: New purulent, foul-smelling drainage, especially with fever and a rising WBC count, suggests infection. Notify the provider.

topics.title: Chemical Mediators
topics.summary: Mast cells and macrophages release the chemicals that cause the classic signs. Too much release causes allergic reactions and anaphylaxis.

sections.heading: Where mediators come from
sections.body: Mediators of inflammation are released by mast cells and macrophages. They produce the vascular changes, pain, and fever of inflammation and draw WBCs to the site. Overactivation of these mediators causes allergic reactions and anaphylaxis.

table.caption: Key inflammatory mediators

Antihistamines relieve itching and hives but do NOT reverse airway swelling or low BP in anaphylaxis
Explains pain and swelling at an injured site

Attract neutrophils and macrophages to the site
Recruit the cells that clear the injury
Vasodilation, pain, fever; also ↑ permeability and WBC attraction

pearls: Prostaglandins cause pain, fever, and swelling, which is why drugs that block them (salicylates, NSAIDs) relieve all three.
A sudden, body-wide burst of mediator release is what anaphylaxis is.

topics.title: Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
topics.summary: Acute inflammation is rapid and resolves once the cause is neutralized. Chronic inflammation lasts months to years and is a major global health threat.

sections.heading: Acute inflammation
sections.body: Acute inflammation is a complex vascular and tissue response that isolates damage and promotes repair. It has a rapid onset (minutes to hours), shows the classic signs (redness, heat, swelling, pain, impaired function), is dominated by neutrophils, and resolves once the cause is neutralized. Acute inflammation may resolve on its own or may require hospitalization.

sections.heading: Chronic inflammation
sections.body: Chronic inflammation lasts months to years. It may follow acute inflammation but often develops independently. It is driven mainly by lymphocytes and macrophages, and ongoing inflammation damages tissue.
bullets: Examples: allergies, COPD, autoimmune diseases (SLE, RA). In RA, joint inflammation leads to deformity.
Linked to aging and obesity.
Common systemic effects: fatigue, loss of appetite, weight loss.

sections.heading: Prevalence and genetics
bullets: Chronic inflammatory diseases are a major global health threat; the WHO calls chronic disease the greatest threat to human health.
About 100 chronic inflammatory diseases have been identified, and 5–7% of the Western population has at least one. The prevalence of acute inflammation is unknown.
About 450 genetic loci are linked to inflammation, and each inflammatory disease has a unique genetic profile. A common pathway is IL-23/IL-17 cytokine regulation.
Nonmodifiable risk factors: genetics, age, family history.

pearls: Chronic inflammation care is about self-management: avoiding triggers, taking medications as prescribed, an anti-inflammatory diet, and exercise. Acute care is about removing the cause and supporting healing.

topics.title: Anaphylaxis
topics.summary: A rapid, life-threatening allergic reaction. Give epinephrine immediately (and activate EMS if outside the hospital); every other drug is secondary.

sections.heading: Pathophysiology
sections.body: Anaphylaxis is overactivation of the inflammatory mediators. In a person who was sensitized by an earlier exposure, the allergen triggers mast cells to release a flood of histamine and other mediators throughout the body. The result is widespread vasodilation and capillary leak (low BP, shock), bronchoconstriction, and airway swelling. Onset is usually within minutes.

sections.heading: Common triggers
bullets: Foods: peanuts, shellfish, milk, eggs
Insect stings
Medications: penicillin, NSAIDs, anesthetics
Latex

sections.heading: Recognition
sections.body: Suspect anaphylaxis when symptoms from more than one body system appear suddenly after a likely trigger. Low BP or wheezing after an exposure is enough, even without hives.
bullets: Airway and breathing: airway swelling (lips, tongue, throat; hoarseness, stridor), wheezing, difficulty breathing
Circulation: low BP, abnormal heart rhythm, dizziness, shock
GI: nausea, vomiting, diarrhea
Skin: hives, itching, cyanosis or pallor

sections.heading: Emergency management
bullets: Remove the trigger: stop the IV drug or infusion (keep the IV line open with normal saline). Call for help: the rapid response team in the hospital, EMS (911) outside the hospital.

Epinephrine IM immediately into the mid-anterolateral thigh (adults usually 0.3–0.5 mg of 1 mg/mL, or an auto-injector, which can go through clothing). It may be repeated every 5–15 minutes if symptoms persist.
Position: lying flat with the legs raised if BP is low; sitting up if breathing is difficult. Do not let the client stand or walk suddenly.
Support the ABCs: high-flow oxygen, IV access with isotonic fluids for low BP, and continuous cardiac and SpO₂ monitoring.
Second-line drugs only after epinephrine: antihistamines, inhaled bronchodilators, corticosteroids. None of them reverses airway swelling or shock.

sections.heading: Prevention and discharge teaching
bullets: Avoid known triggers; read food labels; document the allergy and the type of reaction in the chart; use latex-free equipment for latex-allergic clients.
Carry two epinephrine auto-injectors at all times. Use one at the first sign of a severe reaction, then call 911 even if symptoms improve, because symptoms can return.
Wear a medical alert bracelet, follow a written anaphylaxis action plan, and follow up with an allergist.

pearls: Priority order: remove the trigger, give epinephrine IM, then support airway, breathing, and circulation. Antihistamines never come before epinephrine.
The IM thigh route gives faster absorption than subcutaneous or deltoid injection.
redFlags: Stridor, hoarseness, or tongue swelling means the airway is threatened. Give epinephrine now and call for help.
Low BP or a falling SpO₂ after a new drug, food, sting, or latex exposure is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise.

topics.title: Nursing Assessment and Diagnostic Tests
topics.summary: Local signs, systemic signs, and a handful of labs (WBC with differential, ESR, CRP) tell you how big the fire is.

sections.heading: Observation and interview
sections.body: Look for fever, skin or eye changes, respiratory distress, pain, and the classic signs. Ask about fatigue, appetite loss, recent procedures or surgeries, chronic conditions, medications, diet, and stress.

sections.heading: Physical examination
bullets: Localized: edema, tenderness, redness, heat, decreased function. Outline and measure the area; compare with the other side; check distal circulation.
Systemic (per the course slides): temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) or below 36 °C (96.8 °F), HR above 90/min, RR above 20/min, and WBC above 12,000/mm³ or increased bands.
Systemic findings mean the inflammation is no longer local. Report them promptly, especially when they are new or worsening.

sections.heading: Diagnostic tests
bullets: ESR (erythrocyte sedimentation rate): how fast red cells settle. A faster settling rate = active inflammation. Normal: men 0–15 mm/hr, women 0–20 mm/hr. It is nonspecific and changes slowly.

CRP (C-reactive protein): a protein made by the liver. An ↑ CRP means inflammation. It rises and falls quickly, so it is used to monitor response to treatment, and it is also a cardiac risk marker. Normal is usually below 1.0 mg/dL.
WBC with differential: checks for infection. Normal about 5,000–10,000/mm³. An ↑ WBC with ↑ bands (left shift) suggests acute bacterial infection.
Serum protein electrophoresis: in SLE, ↑ gamma globulin and ↓ albumin.
Chemistry panels: show organ involvement (kidney, liver, muscle).

table.caption: Quick lab interpretation
rows: ↑ bands = left shift → acute bacterial infection
↑ = active inflammation; nonspecific, slow to change
↑ = inflammation; falls quickly with effective treatment

pearls: ESR and CRP tell you that there is inflammation, not where it is or why. They are best used for trends.
A falling CRP means the treatment is working.
redFlags: New fever above 38.5 °C (or below 36 °C), HR above 90, RR above 20, and a rising WBC or bands in a client with a local inflammatory problem means the process has become systemic. Notify the provider promptly.

topics.title: Anti-inflammatory Pharmacology
topics.summary: Goal: reduce inflammation, pain, and fever by blocking prostaglandins, and watch for the predictable harms of each drug class.

sections.heading: Goal and target
sections.body: Drug therapy aims to reduce inflammation, pain, and fever. The main target is prostaglandins, which cause capillary permeability, WBC attraction, pain, and fever. Drug classes: salicylates (OTC), non-opioid analgesics (OTC), NSAIDs (OTC and prescription), corticosteroids (prescription; oral or parenteral for severe cases), and opioids (severe pain only).

sections.heading: Salicylates (aspirin)
bullets: Anti-inflammatory, analgesic, antipyretic, and antiplatelet.
Do not give to children or teens with a viral illness (influenza, chickenpox) because of Reye syndrome (vomiting, lethargy, and confusion progressing to brain and liver injury).
Salicylate toxicity: tinnitus (ringing in the ears), hearing loss, nausea and vomiting, rapid deep breathing, confusion. Check OTC products for hidden aspirin.
Causes GI irritation and bleeding; take with food and avoid with anticoagulants.

sections.heading: NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen)
bullets: GI: stomach irritation, ulcers, and bleeding (black tarry stools, coffee-ground emesis). Take with food or milk, avoid alcohol, do not combine two NSAIDs, and use the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.
Kidney: less blood flow to the kidneys, especially in older or dehydrated clients or those with kidney disease. Report decreased urination or new swelling.
Bleeding: ↑ risk with warfarin and other anticoagulants.
Also cause fluid retention and a rise in BP.

sections.heading: Non-opioid analgesic: acetaminophen
sections.body: Acetaminophen relieves pain and fever but has little anti-inflammatory effect, so it does not reduce swelling. It does not cause GI bleeding. The main risk is liver damage: do not exceed the maximum daily dose (about 4 g/day for healthy adults, less with alcohol use or liver disease), and count acetaminophen in combination products.

sections.heading: Corticosteroids (prednisone, methylprednisolone)
bullets: Powerful anti-inflammatory drugs for severe or chronic inflammation (RA or SLE flares, severe allergic reactions). They suppress the immune response.
Hyperglycemia: monitor blood glucose; clients with diabetes may need more insulin.
Infection risk with masked signs: fever and redness may be blunted. Avoid sick contacts and report early signs of infection.
Other effects: fluid retention and ↑ BP, low potassium, weight gain and a round face, bone loss (osteoporosis), stomach ulcers, mood changes, and slow wound healing.
Take with food in the morning.
Never stop abruptly after long-term use. The body's own cortisol production is suppressed, so sudden withdrawal can cause adrenal insufficiency (weakness, dizziness, low BP). Taper as prescribed.

sections.heading: Opioids
sections.body: Opioids are for severe pain only (see the Comfort module). They do not treat the inflammation itself.

pearls: Black tarry stools, coffee-ground emesis, or new fatigue in a client taking NSAIDs: hold the drug and notify the provider.
'Ringing in my ears' in a client taking high-dose aspirin means salicylate toxicity.
Client with diabetes starting prednisone: expect higher glucose readings and teach the client to check glucose more often.
redFlags: Weakness, dizziness, and low BP after stopping long-term steroids suggest adrenal insufficiency.
Vomiting, lethargy, and confusion in a child recently given aspirin during a viral illness suggest Reye syndrome.

topics.title: Nursing Interventions and Collaborative Care
topics.summary: Reduce edema and movement, feed the repair, teach, prevent, and work with the team (dietitian, physical therapy, surgery).

sections.heading: Independent nursing interventions
bullets: Reduce edema and movement: elevate, ice, position. For an acute soft-tissue injury, use RICE: Rest, Ice (15–20 minutes at a time with a cloth barrier during the first 24–48 hours), Compression (snug, not tight; check distal circulation), Elevation above heart level.
Heat is for later or for chronic stiffness: it increases circulation and relaxes muscles. Do not apply heat to a fresh, acute injury.
Promote healing: adequate fluids, protein, carbohydrates, and vitamins, especially vitamin C.
Comfort and coping: heat or ice as appropriate, positioning, and support during recovery.
Client and family teaching: medications (antibiotics, steroids), nutrition and hydration, wound and dressing care, and activity restrictions until cleared.
Delegation: the UAP may apply a prescribed ice pack, elevate a limb, measure vital signs, and report findings. Assessment, teaching, and evaluation stay with the RN.

sections.heading: Health promotion and modifiable risk factors
bullets: Prevention = avoiding triggers: allergens (dust, pollen, animal dander); food and beverage triggers in Crohn's disease and peptic ulcer disease.
Hand hygiene is the key to preventing infection.
Modifiable risk factors: healthy weight, no smoking, exercise, a high-fiber, low-fat diet, and control of hypertension and diabetes.
Avoid the Western diet (fast food, sugar, low fiber). An anti-inflammatory diet includes fruits, vegetables, fish, whole grains, olive oil, and omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids.
Screening: allergy skin testing to identify allergens; a TSH test to detect Hashimoto thyroiditis.

sections.heading: Collaborative therapies
bullets: Acute inflammation may resolve on its own or may require hospitalization.
Chronic inflammation is linked to aging and obesity; the team may include a dietitian and a physical therapist.
Dietitian: anti-inflammatory diet (↑ omega-3s, antioxidants, probiotics; ↓ saturated fat, cholesterol, and high-glycemic-index foods).
Physical therapy: strength, mobility, and restoring activity.
Complementary approaches: probiotics, acupuncture, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), exercise.

sections.heading: Surgery
sections.body: Surgery is sometimes needed for inflammation, for example colectomy for ulcerative colitis and cholecystectomy for an inflamed gallbladder (appendectomy for appendicitis follows the same principle). The nursing role is preoperative and postoperative care and client teaching: NPO status and fluids before surgery, pain control, monitoring for systemic signs and wound infection, and teaching about wound care, activity, and diet.

pearls: Ice early, heat later. Ice causes vasoconstriction, which limits swelling. Heat causes vasodilation, which helps once the acute phase has passed or for chronic stiffness.
After applying ice or a compression wrap, always check circulation, movement, and sensation distal to it.
redFlags: Numbness, tingling, pallor, coolness, or delayed capillary refill distal to a wrap: loosen the wrap and notify the provider.

topics.title: Lifespan Considerations
topics.summary: Children have small airways and small fluid reserves, pregnancy dampens immunity, and older adults carry more chronic low-grade inflammation.

sections.heading: Children and adolescents
bullets: Airway: large tongue, narrow trachea, and prominent lymphoid tissue increase the risk of obstruction when tissues swell.
Respiratory system: fewer and smaller alveoli and less elastic recoil increase the risk of collapse and respiratory failure.
Renal system: immature kidneys control fluid balance poorly.
Fluid loss is more significant because a child's total fluid volume is smaller. Monitor intake, urine output (wet diapers), mental status, and capillary refill.
Cardiac response: the sympathetic response is weaker, and the slides note that tachycardia can be a late sign of hypovolemia, so do not wait for vital-sign changes before acting on fluid losses.
GI and nutrition: ↓ absorption affects growth, weight, and strength.
Immune system: more pro-inflammatory mediators and less ability to dampen inflammation.
Care: child life specialists, play therapy, and noninvasive imaging when possible. Dose drugs by weight, and do not give aspirin for a viral illness (Reye syndrome).

sections.heading: Pregnancy
bullets: Pregnancy dampens the immune system to protect the fetus.
It may cause hypersensitivity to harmless (nonpathogenic) stimuli and can contribute to chronic inflammatory diseases.
Preeclampsia is an inflammation-mediated hypertensive disorder. A severe headache or visual changes must be reported right away.

sections.heading: Older adults
bullets: Raised inflammatory markers (CRP, IL-6, TNF-α) are common, and they are higher in frail than in non-frail adults.
They are linked to more illness, more comorbidities, and more hospitalizations.
They can be improved with diet and resistance training.
Infection may present atypically: little or no fever, and instead new confusion, falls, or loss of appetite. Compare findings with the client's own baseline.

pearls: Older adult with new confusion: think infection or inflammation before assuming dementia.
In a young child with fever, vomiting, or diarrhea, count the wet diapers. Urine output is an early, easy measure of fluid balance.
redFlags: A child with lethargy, delayed capillary refill, and no wet diapers for many hours needs immediate attention.
A pregnant client with preeclampsia who reports a severe headache or vision changes needs immediate provider notification.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client has a red, warm area on the forearm 1 day after a minor burn. The client asks why the area looks red and feels hot. Which physiologic process should the nurse include in the explanation?
options: Increased capillary permeability allowing plasma to leak into the tissue
Stimulation of nerve endings by bradykinin and prostaglandins
Arteriolar vasodilation that increases blood flow to the injured area
Migration of neutrophils out of the vessels toward the injury
optionRationales: Increased permeability causes swelling (edema), not redness or heat.
Nerve stimulation by bradykinin and prostaglandins explains pain, not redness or warmth.
Correct. Vasodilation causes hyperemia, and the extra blood flow produces redness (rubor) and heat (calor).
Neutrophil migration is part of the cellular response and phagocytosis. It does not directly cause redness or heat.
questions.rationale: Mediators such as histamine and prostaglandins dilate arterioles. The resulting hyperemia makes the area red and warm. Swelling comes from increased permeability, and pain from mediator stimulation of nerves plus tissue pressure.
questions.takeaway: Redness and heat = vasodilation; swelling = permeability; pain = bradykinin, prostaglandins, and pressure.
questions.hintContent: Think about what happens to blood flow in an injured area and which vascular change brings more warm blood to the surface.
questions.hintStrategy: Match each option to the single cardinal sign it explains. Only one mechanism accounts for BOTH findings in the stem.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client who sprained the right ankle 6 hours ago has an elastic compression wrap in place. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider immediately?
options: Pale, cool toes on the right foot with capillary refill of 5 seconds
Warmth and swelling over the lateral malleolus with tenderness
Pain rated 5/10 that increases when the client bears weight on the foot
Limited ability to rotate the ankle because of pain and stiffness
optionRationales: Correct. Pale, cool toes with delayed capillary refill mean impaired circulation distal to the injury, often from a wrap that is too tight as swelling increases. This needs immediate action.
Warmth, swelling, and tenderness at the injury site are expected cardinal signs of acute inflammation.
Moderate pain that worsens with weight bearing is expected after a sprain.
Loss of function is a classic sign of inflammation and is expected.
questions.rationale: The five cardinal signs are expected at the injury site. Signs of impaired circulation distal to the injury or wrap (pallor, coolness, delayed capillary refill, numbness) are not expected. They point to vascular compromise that could cause tissue ischemia.
questions.takeaway: Cardinal signs at the site are expected; circulation problems distal to it are an emergency.
questions.hintContent: Recall the five cardinal signs and where on the limb they appear. Decide whether each finding is at the injury site or beyond it.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide which findings are expected at the site of an acute injury and which suggest a problem developing elsewhere in the limb.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Stage 1 – Vascular & Cellular Response
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: Moments after cutting a finger on a kitchen knife, a client noticed the skin around the cut looked pale. Within a few minutes it turned red and warm. The client asks the nurse why it was pale at first. Which explanation is accurate?
options: Plasma leaked out of the capillaries and diluted the blood in the area
Neutrophils collected in the tissue and displaced the blood
Scar tissue began forming immediately around the wound
The small arteries briefly constricted before dilating
optionRationales: Increased capillary permeability causes swelling. It does not cause pallor, and it follows vasodilation.
Neutrophils arrive over hours and do not cause immediate pallor.
Scar formation occurs in the reparative phase, days to weeks later.
Correct. A transient arteriolar vasoconstriction lasting seconds happens first (pallor). It is followed by vasodilation (hyperemia), which makes the area red and warm.
questions.rationale: Stage 1 of inflammation begins with a momentary vasoconstriction. Vasodilation (hyperemia) and increased capillary permeability follow quickly, producing redness, heat, and swelling. The cellular response and later repair come after.
questions.takeaway: Constrict (seconds) → dilate → leak → cells → repair.
questions.hintContent: Recall the very first thing arterioles do in the seconds after injury, before they dilate.
questions.hintStrategy: The client's observation has two parts, pale first and red later. Pick the option that explains the pale phase.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: While changing a dressing on a client's abdominal incision, the nurse finds thick, opaque, yellow-green drainage with a foul odor. How should the nurse document the drainage?
options: Serous
Serosanguineous
Purulent
Fibrinous
optionRationales: Serous exudate is clear to straw-colored and thin.
Serosanguineous exudate is thin, watery, and pale pink.
Correct. Thick, opaque, yellow-green, malodorous drainage is purulent. It contains WBCs, dead tissue, and bacteria and indicates infection.
Fibrinous exudate is thick and sticky from fibrin and is typical of serous membranes (pericarditis), not an infected incision.
questions.rationale: Purulent exudate (pus) is thick and opaque, may be yellow, green, or tan, and often smells. It signals bacterial infection, so the nurse should document it, obtain a culture if prescribed, and notify the provider.
questions.takeaway: Thick, colored, and smelly = purulent = infection.
questions.hintContent: Review what each exudate type looks like: clarity, thickness, color, and odor.
questions.hintStrategy: Link each descriptor in the stem (thick, opaque, colored, odor) to the exudate type that has all of them.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: Twelve hours after a hip replacement, the dressing over a client's incision has a 3 cm area of thin, watery, pale pink drainage. Vital signs: T 37.4 °C (99.3 °F), HR 84, BP 126/74. What is the nurse's most appropriate action?
options: Notify the surgeon of possible postoperative hemorrhage from the hip
Continue to monitor the amount and character of the drainage
Obtain a culture of the drainage and send it to the laboratory
Remove the dressing and leave the incision open to air
optionRationales: Hemorrhage would produce large amounts of bright red (sanguineous) drainage, often with tachycardia and hypotension.
Correct. Small amounts of serosanguineous drainage are expected early after surgery. The nurse should continue to monitor for changes in amount or character.
A culture is indicated for purulent drainage or signs of infection, which are not present.
The drainage is expected, and the dressing protects the fresh incision. Removing it is not indicated by this finding.
questions.rationale: Serosanguineous exudate (thin, pale pink) is the expected drainage in the early postoperative period and should decrease and lighten over time. Stable vital signs support an expected finding.
questions.takeaway: Pale pink and thin early after surgery = expected; keep monitoring the trend.
questions.hintContent: Remember which type of drainage is normal in the first postoperative days and how it should change over time.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide first whether the drainage described is expected at this point after surgery; then use the vital signs to confirm or refute that impression.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with acute tendinitis asks how ibuprofen will help. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
options: It blocks histamine receptors so the blood vessels stop leaking fluid.
It kills the bacteria that are causing the tendon to become inflamed.
It suppresses the immune system so white blood cells stop reaching the tendon.
It lowers production of prostaglandins that cause pain, swelling, and fever.
optionRationales: Blocking histamine receptors is how antihistamines work, not NSAIDs.
NSAIDs have no antibacterial action, and tendinitis is usually not infectious.
Broad immune suppression describes corticosteroids, not NSAIDs.
Correct. NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase (COX), which lowers prostaglandin synthesis and so reduces pain, swelling, and fever.
questions.rationale: Prostaglandins cause vasodilation, increased permeability, pain, and fever. NSAIDs inhibit COX enzymes, which lowers prostaglandin levels. This is also why NSAIDs reduce protection of the stomach lining and blood flow to the kidneys.
questions.takeaway: NSAIDs → block COX → ↓ prostaglandins → ↓ pain, fever, and swelling (and ↓ GI and renal protection).
questions.hintContent: Remember the enzyme NSAIDs inhibit and the mediator that enzyme produces.
questions.hintStrategy: Rule out options that describe other drug classes (antihistamines, antibiotics, corticosteroids).

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client's healing leg wound 10 days after debridement. Which wound bed finding indicates the reparative phase is progressing as expected?
options: Beefy red, moist, granular tissue that bleeds slightly when touched
Pale pink, dry tissue with a thin gray film spread across the entire surface
Yellow, stringy tissue that adheres firmly to the wound base
Black, leathery tissue covering most of the wound surface
optionRationales: Correct. Healthy granulation tissue is beefy red, moist, and bumpy. It bleeds easily because it contains many new capillaries.
Pale, dry tissue with a gray film suggests poor perfusion or infection.
Yellow, stringy tissue is slough (devitalized tissue) that delays healing.
Black, leathery tissue is eschar (necrotic tissue).
questions.rationale: Granulation tissue is fragile, highly vascular connective tissue that fills the wound during repair. It is the expected finding in a healing wound and should be protected with a moist, non-adherent dressing.
questions.takeaway: Beefy red, moist, and bleeds easily = healthy granulation.
questions.hintContent: Picture healthy granulation tissue: color, moisture, texture, and why it bleeds easily.
questions.hintStrategy: You are evaluating progress. Choose the tissue type that reflects repair, not dead or devitalized tissue.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: Ten minutes after an IV infusion of piperacillin-tazobactam starts, a client reports 'my throat feels tight.' The nurse notes generalized hives and wheezing; BP is 84/50 mm Hg and SpO₂ is 90%. What should the nurse do first?
options: Administer diphenhydramine IV as prescribed
Stop the antibiotic infusion
Raise the head of the bed to high Fowler's position
Obtain a set of blood cultures before the next dose
optionRationales: Diphenhydramine is a second-line adjunct. It does not reverse airway edema or shock and never comes before stopping the trigger and giving epinephrine.
Correct. Stopping the infusion removes the allergen so no more of it enters the circulation. The nurse then calls for help and gives IM epinephrine immediately.
Hypotension calls for supine positioning with legs elevated. Positioning also does not remove the cause.
Blood cultures do not address a life-threatening allergic reaction.
questions.rationale: With an IV-drug-triggered anaphylactic reaction, the first action is to stop the offending infusion (keeping the line open with normal saline). Epinephrine IM follows immediately, along with a call for the rapid response team. Removing the trigger takes seconds and prevents further exposure.
questions.takeaway: IV drug reaction: stop the infusion → call for help → epinephrine IM.
questions.hintContent: Think about how the allergen is still getting into the client and what stops more of it from entering.
questions.hintStrategy: The stem asks what to do FIRST. Consider whether the client is still being exposed to the trigger before choosing among the treatments.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse has stopped an IV antibiotic infusion in an adult client who developed stridor, hives, and BP 80/48 mm Hg. The rapid response team has been called. Which prescribed medication should the nurse give first?
options: Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV push over 1 to 2 minutes
Albuterol 2.5 mg in 3 mL saline via nebulizer
Epinephrine 0.5 mg IM in the mid-anterolateral thigh
Famotidine 20 mg IV push diluted in 10 mL saline
optionRationales: Corticosteroids act slowly (hours) and do not treat acute airway or circulatory compromise.
Albuterol treats bronchospasm but not laryngeal edema or hypotension. It is an adjunct.
Correct. IM epinephrine (1 mg/mL concentration) is first-line. Its alpha effects reverse vasodilation and edema, and its beta-2 effects relieve bronchospasm. The thigh gives the fastest absorption.
H2 blockers are adjuncts for skin and GI symptoms only.
questions.rationale: Epinephrine is the only drug that treats every life-threatening feature of anaphylaxis: airway edema, bronchoconstriction, and shock. Give 0.01 mg/kg (adult max 0.5 mg) of 1 mg/mL IM into the vastus lateralis, repeating every 5–15 minutes as needed.
questions.takeaway: Epinephrine IM in the thigh first; everything else is an adjunct.
questions.hintContent: Recall which drug reverses vasodilation, capillary leak, and bronchospasm all at once.
questions.hintStrategy: Several options are real anaphylaxis drugs. Separate first-line from adjunct by asking which one treats the airway AND the blood pressure.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client received epinephrine IM for anaphylaxis after a bee sting. The client is breathing without difficulty but reports feeling lightheaded; BP is 88/54 mm Hg. How should the nurse position the client?
options: Supine with the legs elevated
High Fowler's position
Standing, supported, to walk to the stretcher
Prone with the head turned to the side
optionRationales: Correct. Lying flat with the legs raised increases venous return and preload, which supports BP in distributive shock.
Sitting upright is for clients whose main problem is breathing difficulty. Here it would worsen hypotension.
Standing or walking during anaphylaxis can cause sudden cardiovascular collapse (the 'empty ventricle').
Prone positioning does not support circulation and hinders assessment.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis causes massive vasodilation and fluid leak. A hypotensive client without respiratory distress should be kept supine with the legs elevated. A dyspneic client may sit up with the legs extended, and a pregnant client should lie on her left side.
questions.takeaway: Hypotensive anaphylaxis: flat with legs up; never stand or walk.
questions.hintContent: Think about how gravity and venous return affect blood pressure in distributive shock.
questions.hintStrategy: Note that the client is breathing comfortably. The problem to solve is the blood pressure, not breathing.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client who was treated for anaphylaxis after a yellow jacket sting is being discharged with epinephrine auto-injectors and a referral to an allergist. Which statement by the client indicates understanding of the discharge teaching?
options: “I'll wear closed shoes outside and keep my drinks covered at picnics.”
“My next sting will probably be milder because my body has reacted once.”
“I can take an antihistamine before yard work instead of carrying epinephrine.”
“I only need to carry my auto-injector during the warm summer months.”
optionRationales: Correct. Avoiding exposure is the first line of prevention. Stinging insects nest in the ground and are drawn to open sweet drinks, so closed shoes and covered drinks lower the chance of another sting.
Needs further teaching. A client who has had a systemic reaction to a sting is at risk for an equally or more severe reaction with the next sting; the sensitivity does not fade after one reaction.
Needs further teaching. Antihistamines do not prevent or treat airway edema or shock. Epinephrine must be carried at all times.
Needs further teaching. Stings can happen in any season (indoors, during warm spells, or while traveling), so the auto-injector is carried at all times.
questions.rationale: Prevention after insect-sting anaphylaxis combines avoiding triggers (closed shoes, covered drinks, avoiding perfumes and bright floral clothing outdoors, professional nest removal), carrying two epinephrine auto-injectors at all times, and allergist evaluation for venom immunotherapy, which greatly lowers the risk of future systemic reactions.
questions.takeaway: After sting anaphylaxis: avoid triggers, carry epinephrine always, and see an allergist.
questions.hintContent: Recall how avoiding triggers fits into health promotion for allergies and whether the risk of anaphylaxis fades after one reaction.
questions.hintStrategy: This item asks for a statement that shows understanding. Test each statement against what would keep the client safe at the next exposure.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with an infected finger asks how the body 'marks' bacteria so the white blood cells can destroy them. The nurse explains that a group of more than 20 plasma proteins helps dilate vessels and helps white blood cells engulf the bacteria. Which mediator is the nurse describing?
options: Bradykinin
Leukotrienes
Histamine
Complement
optionRationales: Bradykinin causes vessel dilation, pain, and increased permeability. It is a single peptide, not a group of proteins, and does not aid phagocytosis.
Leukotrienes attract neutrophils and macrophages to the site, but they are not a group of plasma proteins that aid phagocytosis.
Histamine (with heparin) increases blood flow and prevents clotting at the site. It does not help WBCs engulf microbes.
Correct. Complement is a system of more than 20 plasma proteins that aids vessel dilation and phagocytosis.
questions.rationale: Mediators are released by mast cells and macrophages, and each has a characteristic job. Complement, a group of more than 20 proteins, aids vessel dilation and phagocytosis. Histamine and heparin increase blood flow and prevent clotting, bradykinin causes dilation, pain, and permeability, leukotrienes attract neutrophils and macrophages, and prostaglandins cause vasodilation, pain, and fever.
questions.takeaway: Complement = >20 proteins that aid dilation and phagocytosis.
questions.hintContent: Recall the key mediators of inflammation and the main effect of each one.
questions.hintStrategy: Two cues in the stem narrow the choice: a 'group of proteins' and 'helps WBCs engulf.' Eliminate mediators known for a different main effect.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client admitted with suspected appendicitis has these results: WBC 16,800/mm³, neutrophils 82%, bands 14%. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
options: Expected results after a viral illness
An allergic reaction to the admission medications
Bone marrow suppression requiring neutropenic precautions
A left shift suggesting an acute bacterial infection
optionRationales: Viral infections usually raise lymphocytes, not bands.
Allergic responses typically raise eosinophils.
A WBC of 16,800 is elevated, not suppressed. Neutropenic precautions are for low counts.
Correct. Leukocytosis with increased immature neutrophils (bands above 10%) is a left shift. It shows the marrow is releasing neutrophils early to fight acute bacterial infection.
questions.rationale: A left shift, meaning more bands on the differential, reflects an acute demand for neutrophils, most often from bacterial infection or severe inflammation. In appendicitis, a rising band count can also hint at perforation.
questions.takeaway: ↑ bands = left shift = acute bacterial infection.
questions.hintContent: Recall what bands are and what an increase in immature neutrophils means.
questions.hintStrategy: Look at the differential, not just the total WBC. Each distractor matches a different WBC pattern.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis started a new disease-modifying drug 8 weeks ago. Refer to the Laboratory Results. How should the nurse interpret the change in the C-reactive protein (CRP)?
options: The inflammation is decreasing, suggesting the treatment is effective.
The client has developed an infection that the drug is masking.
The liver is being damaged by the new medication and makes less CRP.
The client's risk of an allergic or anaphylactic reaction has increased.
optionRationales: Correct. CRP is an acute-phase protein that falls quickly as inflammation subsides, which makes it useful for monitoring response to therapy. The ESR is falling more slowly, as expected.
Infection would raise CRP, not lower it, and the WBC is normal.
CRP is made by the liver, but a falling CRP does not indicate liver injury, and the ALT is unchanged and normal.
CRP does not predict allergic reactions or anaphylaxis.
questions.rationale: CRP is made by the liver in response to inflammatory cytokines (IL-6). It rises within hours and falls quickly when inflammation resolves, so serial values help evaluate treatment. A value below about 1.0 mg/dL is generally within normal limits.
questions.takeaway: Falling CRP = cooling inflammation = treatment working.
questions.hintContent: Remember how quickly CRP responds to changes in inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Look at the direction of change (before vs. after treatment) and decide what it says about the therapy.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The nurse receives report on four clients. Which client should the nurse assess first?
options: A client 2 days after knee arthroscopy with warmth and mild swelling at the incision; T 37.3 °C (99.1 °F)
A client with psoriasis with red, scaly plaques on the elbows who is asking for a topical steroid
A client 1 day after bowel surgery with T 38.9 °C (102 °F), HR 118, RR 26, and WBC 15,500/mm³
A client with a sprained wrist rating pain 6/10 who is due for oral ibuprofen
optionRationales: Mild warmth and swelling with a near-normal temperature is an expected local inflammatory response after surgery.
Chronic psoriasis plaques are a stable, chronic finding.

Correct. This client has systemic signs of inflammation (temperature above 38.5 °C, HR above 90, RR above 20, WBC above 12,000) after bowel surgery, which suggests a serious complication such as infection spreading in the abdomen. These findings are unstable and systemic.
Moderate pain from a sprain is expected. The medication can be given after the unstable client is seen.
questions.rationale: Systemic signs of inflammation after abdominal surgery signal a possibly life-threatening complication. Systemic, unstable findings take priority over expected local signs and chronic, stable conditions.
questions.takeaway: Systemic beats local; unstable beats stable.
questions.hintContent: Review the systemic signs of inflammation from the nursing assessment: temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and WBC count.
questions.hintStrategy: Sort the clients into expected/stable and unexpected/systemic. The priority is the client whose findings affect several body systems.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The parent of an 8-year-old with influenza asks whether the child can take aspirin for fever and body aches. Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “Yes, give a children's dose of aspirin every 4 hours as needed for aches.”
“Aspirin is fine as long as you give it with food to protect the stomach.”
“Alternate the aspirin with ibuprofen every 3 hours to keep the fever down.”
“Avoid aspirin; it is linked to Reye syndrome with viral illnesses.”
optionRationales: Aspirin is contraindicated in children and teens with viral illnesses.
Food reduces GI upset but does not prevent Reye syndrome.
Any aspirin exposure during a viral illness carries the risk of Reye syndrome.
Correct. Aspirin during influenza or varicella in anyone under 19 is linked to Reye syndrome (encephalopathy and liver failure). Acetaminophen or ibuprofen at weight-based doses is preferred.
questions.rationale: Reye syndrome is a rare but often fatal condition causing acute encephalopathy and fatty liver after aspirin use during a viral infection in children and teens. Teach families to check OTC labels for salicylates (e.g., bismuth subsalicylate).
questions.takeaway: Kids plus viral illness plus aspirin = Reye syndrome risk. Avoid it.
questions.hintContent: Recall the syndrome linked to salicylates in children and teens with influenza or chickenpox.
questions.hintStrategy: The client's age and the viral illness are the key cues. Pick the answer that addresses that specific risk, not general GI protection.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A 74-year-old client with osteoarthritis has taken naproxen 500 mg twice daily for 3 months. The client reports feeling tired and having 'black, sticky stools.' Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Teach the client to take naproxen with milk to reduce stomach irritation
Hold the next naproxen dose and notify the provider
Suggest the client increase dietary fiber and fluids
Reassure the client that dark stools are a common side effect of NSAIDs
optionRationales: Taking the drug with milk is prevention teaching. It does not address a possible active GI bleed.
Correct. Melena and fatigue suggest upper GI bleeding with blood loss. The NSAID should be held and the provider notified for prompt evaluation.
Fiber and fluids address constipation, not melena.
Black, tarry stools are not a benign side effect of NSAIDs (unlike those from iron or bismuth). Reassurance delays care.
questions.rationale: NSAIDs reduce the prostaglandins that protect the stomach lining, which increases the risk of ulcers and bleeding, and older age increases that risk. Melena and fatigue require holding the drug and prompt evaluation.
questions.takeaway: NSAID plus black tarry stools → hold the drug and notify the provider.
questions.hintContent: Think about what NSAIDs do to the gastric lining and what black, sticky stool means.
questions.hintStrategy: Decide whether this is a teaching problem or a possible active complication. Act on the complication first.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client has taken prednisone 40 mg daily for 4 weeks for an asthma flare. The client says, “I feel great now, so I'm going to stop the prednisone tomorrow.” Which response by the nurse is best?
options: “That's fine, since your breathing symptoms have fully resolved now.”
“Skip every other day for a week, and then stop taking it completely.”
“Stopping suddenly is unsafe; the dose must be tapered as prescribed.”
“Keep taking it until you finish the bottle, and then you can stop.”
optionRationales: Stopping abruptly after 4 weeks of use risks adrenal insufficiency.
A self-designed schedule is unsafe. Tapering must follow the provider's prescription.
Correct. Long-term steroid use suppresses the HPA axis. Abrupt withdrawal can cause adrenal crisis (hypotension, hypoglycemia, shock), so the dose is tapered gradually.
Finishing the bottle and then stopping is still abrupt withdrawal unless the prescription is a taper.
questions.rationale: Exogenous corticosteroids given for more than about 2 weeks suppress the body's own cortisol production. A gradual taper lets the adrenal glands recover. Teach the client the signs of adrenal insufficiency: weakness, dizziness, nausea, and hypotension.
questions.takeaway: Long-term steroids: taper, never stop abruptly.
questions.hintContent: Recall what long-term steroid therapy does to the body's own cortisol production.
questions.hintStrategy: Consider how long the client has taken the drug. Choose the response that prevents harm and explains why.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes controlled with metformin is started on methylprednisolone for a severe flare of rheumatoid arthritis. Which finding should the nurse anticipate and monitor for?
options: Blood glucose below 70 mg/dL
Serum potassium above 5.0 mEq/L
Heart rate below 60 beats/min
Blood glucose above 180 mg/dL
optionRationales: Corticosteroids raise, not lower, blood glucose.
Corticosteroids cause potassium loss (hypokalemia), not hyperkalemia.
Bradycardia is not a typical corticosteroid effect.
Correct. Glucocorticoids increase gluconeogenesis and insulin resistance, causing hyperglycemia. The client may need more frequent glucose checks and temporary insulin.
questions.rationale: Steroid-induced hyperglycemia is common, especially in clients with diabetes. The nurse monitors blood glucose and teaches the client about symptoms of high blood sugar.
questions.takeaway: Steroids raise glucose, lower potassium, and mask infection.
questions.hintContent: Remember how glucocorticoids affect gluconeogenesis and insulin sensitivity.
questions.hintStrategy: The client's diabetes is the key cue. Ask which lab change would matter most for this client.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client sprained an ankle playing basketball 2 hours ago. Which instruction about cold therapy is correct?
options: Apply a heating pad for 30 minutes to increase circulation
Apply ice wrapped in a cloth for 15–20 minutes at a time
Place the ice directly on the skin until the area is numb
Alternate heat and ice every 10 minutes for the first day
optionRationales: Heat causes vasodilation and increases swelling in an acute injury. It is used after 48 hours.
Correct. Cold causes vasoconstriction, which limits swelling, bleeding, and pain. Use a barrier and limit each application to 15–20 minutes to prevent tissue injury.
Direct ice or prolonged application can cause frostbite or nerve injury.
Heat is avoided during the first 24–48 hours.
questions.rationale: RICE (rest, ice, compression, elevation) limits the vascular phase of acute inflammation. Ice is applied with a barrier for 15–20 minutes, every few hours, for the first 24–48 hours.
questions.takeaway: Acute injury: ice with a barrier, 15–20 min; heat only after 48 h.
questions.hintContent: Remember whether cold or heat limits swelling in the first 24–48 hours, and why.
questions.hintStrategy: Check each option for the type of therapy, the duration, and skin protection. Only one gets all three right.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Lifespan Considerations – Older Adults
questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: An 84-year-old resident of a long-term care facility has a temperature of 37.1 °C (98.8 °F) and a urinalysis positive for leukocytes and nitrites. Which finding is the most likely indicator of infection in this client?
options: New-onset confusion and agitation since yesterday
A chronic, dry, nonproductive cough present for several years
Mild ankle edema that appears at the end of each day
A regular heart rate of 72 beats/min at rest
optionRationales: Correct. Older adults often have a blunted fever response. Acute confusion (delirium) is a common and sometimes the only sign of infection such as a UTI.
A chronic cough is a baseline finding and does not suggest an acute infection.
Dependent edema at the end of the day is a common, chronic finding in older adults.
A heart rate of 72 is within normal limits.
questions.rationale: Aging blunts the classic inflammatory response (lower baseline temperature, less fever, fewer local signs). New or sudden changes in mental status, falls, or loss of appetite may be the first clue to infection.
questions.takeaway: Older adult plus new confusion = look for infection.
questions.hintContent: Recall how aging changes the fever response and the classic presentation of infection.
questions.hintStrategy: Consider how aging changes the way infection presents, and compare each finding with what would be baseline for this client.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: A client with rheumatoid arthritis asks which meal best fits an anti-inflammatory eating pattern. Which choice should the nurse recommend?
options: Fried chicken sandwich with french fries and a regular soda
Grilled salmon with leafy greens, quinoa, and olive oil
Bacon cheeseburger on a white bun with a chocolate milkshake
White pasta with cream sauce and sliced Italian sausage
optionRationales: Fried foods, refined carbohydrates, and sugary drinks are typical of the pro-inflammatory Western diet.
Correct. Fatty fish (omega-3s), vegetables, whole grains, and olive oil are core anti-inflammatory foods.
High in saturated fat and sugar, which are pro-inflammatory.
Refined carbohydrates, saturated fat, and processed meat promote inflammation.
questions.rationale: An anti-inflammatory diet emphasizes fruits, vegetables, whole grains, fish rich in omega-3 fatty acids, nuts, and olive oil, and limits fast food, sugar, saturated fat, and processed meats. Clients with chronic inflammatory disease can also track and avoid their own trigger foods, with help from a dietitian.
questions.takeaway: Fish, greens, whole grains, and olive oil calm inflammation.
questions.hintContent: Recall the foods emphasized in an anti-inflammatory eating pattern (omega-3s, whole grains, vegetables, olive oil).
questions.hintStrategy: Rule out the meals that match the Western diet: fried, processed, high in sugar and saturated fat.

questions.clientNeed: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Management of Care
questions.stem: The RN is caring for a client admitted with cellulitis of the left lower leg. Which task is appropriate to delegate to the unlicensed assistive personnel (UAP)?
options: Outlining the margins of the redness with a skin marker to track spread
Evaluating whether the pain has improved after the IV analgesic
Teaching the client the signs of worsening infection to report
Elevating the client's left leg on pillows
optionRationales: Marking and interpreting the margins of erythema is assessment, which is an RN responsibility.
Evaluating the response to medication is an RN responsibility.
Teaching is an RN responsibility.
Correct. Positioning and elevating an extremity as prescribed is a routine, noninvasive task within the UAP's scope.
questions.rationale: The RN cannot delegate assessment, teaching, evaluation, or nursing judgment. Routine comfort measures such as elevation, repositioning, and vital sign measurement on stable clients can be delegated, and the UAP reports abnormal findings back.
questions.takeaway: UAP: positioning, ice packs, vital signs. RN: assess, teach, evaluate.
questions.hintContent: Recall which nursing activities cannot be delegated: assess, teach, evaluate, and judge.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask whether it needs nursing judgment or is a routine task with a predictable outcome.

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 52-year-old client has had bilateral hand joint swelling and morning stiffness lasting more than an hour for 3 years. The hands now show ulnar deviation, and the ESR is 48 mm/hr. Which process best explains these findings?
options: Acute inflammation that will resolve once the trigger is removed
Localized bacterial infection that needs incision and drainage
Chronic inflammation with ongoing tissue destruction
An immediate allergic (IgE-mediated) hypersensitivity reaction
optionRationales: Acute inflammation begins within minutes to hours and resolves. It does not cause deformity over years.
Nothing in the stem suggests an abscess or purulent collection.
Correct. Years of symmetric joint inflammation with deformity is rheumatoid arthritis, a chronic inflammation driven by lymphocytes and macrophages that destroys tissue and causes fibrosis.
IgE-mediated reactions occur within minutes of an allergen exposure and do not cause progressive joint deformity.
questions.rationale: Chronic inflammation lasts months to years, often arises from autoimmunity rather than following acute inflammation, and causes progressive tissue destruction and fibrosis. RA is the classic example. An elevated ESR reflects the ongoing inflammatory activity.
questions.takeaway: Chronic = months to years, lymphocytes and macrophages, tissue destruction.
questions.hintContent: Recall how long each type of inflammation lasts and which one causes permanent structural change.
questions.hintStrategy: Use the duration and the deformity in the stem to pick the process, then rule out the options that describe short-lived responses.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A 3-year-old is brought to the ED after eating a cookie containing peanuts. The child has hives on the face and chest, a hoarse cry, and inspiratory stridor. SpO₂ is 93% and BP is 96/60 mm Hg. Which is the nurse's priority concern?
options: Fluid volume deficit related to vomiting
Airway obstruction from laryngeal edema
Impaired skin integrity from urticaria
Anxiety of the parents
optionRationales: No vomiting is described. Circulation matters, but the airway comes first.
Correct. Hoarseness and stridor mean upper airway edema. A child's small, narrow airway and large tongue mean slight swelling can cause complete obstruction. Epinephrine IM is needed immediately.
Hives are uncomfortable but not life-threatening.
Parental anxiety is psychosocial and a lower priority than airway.
questions.rationale: The ABCs guide priority. Children's anatomy (narrow trachea, large tongue, prominent lymphoid tissue) increases the risk of obstruction from inflammatory edema. Stridor is a sign of significant upper airway narrowing.
questions.takeaway: Child plus stridor plus allergen = airway emergency. Give epinephrine now.
questions.hintContent: Think about how a child's airway anatomy changes the impact of even small amounts of swelling.
questions.hintStrategy: Apply the ABCs to the cues in the stem and decide which body system is most immediately threatened.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing a client's inflamed knee. Which findings are cardinal signs of acute inflammation? Select all that apply.
options: Redness over the joint
Warmth to the touch
Swelling of the joint
Cyanosis of the toes
Decreased range of motion
Bradycardia
optionRationales: Correct. Redness (rubor) comes from vasodilation.
Correct. Heat (calor) comes from increased blood flow.
Correct. Swelling (tumor) comes from increased capillary permeability.
Cyanosis reflects poor oxygenation or perfusion and is not a sign of inflammation.
Correct. Loss of function (functio laesa) comes from pain and swelling.
Inflammation and fever tend to cause tachycardia, not bradycardia.
questions.rationale: The five cardinal signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function. Cyanosis and bradycardia are not part of the inflammatory response and would suggest another problem.
questions.takeaway: Red, hot, swollen, painful, and not working right.
questions.hintContent: Recall the five cardinal signs by their Latin names and what each one looks like at the bedside.
questions.hintStrategy: Evaluate each option on its own: is it caused by the local inflammatory response, or does it point to another problem?

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client received the first dose of IV penicillin G 5 minutes ago. Which findings should make the nurse suspect anaphylaxis? Select all that apply.
options: Hoarse voice and a feeling of throat tightness
Generalized urticaria and flushing
BP 82/46 mm Hg with HR 124
BP 168/94 mm Hg with HR 58
Wheezing with SpO₂ of 89%
Increased urine output
optionRationales: Correct. Laryngeal edema threatens the airway.
Correct. Skin involvement from histamine release is common.
Correct. Distributive shock (hypotension with compensatory tachycardia) comes from vasodilation and capillary leak.
Hypertension with bradycardia is not the typical pattern of anaphylaxis.
Correct. Bronchoconstriction and airway edema cause wheezing and hypoxemia.
Shock decreases renal perfusion and urine output.
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis involves multiple systems: skin (hives, flushing), respiratory (stridor, wheeze, hypoxia), cardiovascular (hypotension, tachycardia), and GI. Onset within minutes of an IV trigger is typical.
questions.takeaway: Skin plus airway or breathing plus low BP after exposure = anaphylaxis.
questions.hintContent: Think about the body systems anaphylaxis affects and what widespread vasodilation does to vital signs and perfusion.
questions.hintStrategy: Take each vital sign pattern on its own and ask whether it matches distributive shock.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia is being assessed for signs that the inflammation has become systemic. Which assessment findings are systemic signs of inflammation? Select all that apply.
options: Temperature 39.1 °C (102.4 °F)
Heart rate 104 beats/min
Respiratory rate 18 breaths/min
WBC 14,600/mm³
BP 118/76 mm Hg
Serum sodium 138 mEq/L
optionRationales: Correct. A temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) is a systemic sign.
Correct. Heart rate above 90/min meets the criterion.
The criterion is RR above 20/min, so 18 does not meet it.
Correct. A WBC above 12,000/mm³ (or increased bands) is a systemic sign.
Blood pressure is not one of the systemic signs listed; this value is normal.
Sodium is not one of the systemic signs, and this value is normal.
questions.rationale: The course lists these systemic signs: temperature above 38.5 °C (101.3 °F) or below 36 °C (96.8 °F), HR above 90, RR above 20, and WBC above 12,000/mm³ or increased bands. Blood pressure and sodium are not on the list.
questions.takeaway: Systemic inflammation: temperature, HR, RR, and WBC or bands.
questions.hintContent: Review the four systemic findings in the nursing assessment and their cutoffs.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each value with its exact cutoff. Ignore values that are not part of the list.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client who will take ibuprofen 600 mg three times daily for 2 weeks for bursitis. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: Take each dose with food or milk.
Report black, tarry stools or vomit that looks like coffee grounds.
Limit or avoid alcohol while taking this medication.
Take it on an empty stomach for faster pain relief.
It is safe to add an over-the-counter naproxen product for extra relief.
Report a decrease in urination or new swelling of the ankles.
optionRationales: Correct. Food reduces GI irritation.
Correct. These are signs of GI bleeding.
Correct. Alcohol adds to the risk of GI bleeding.
An empty stomach increases GI irritation and ulcer risk.
Combining two NSAIDs increases GI and renal toxicity without added benefit.
Correct. NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow and cause fluid retention, so these may signal kidney injury.
questions.rationale: NSAID teaching focuses on GI protection and bleeding signs, renal effects, cardiovascular risk (BP, edema), avoiding duplicate NSAIDs, and using the lowest effective dose for the shortest time.
questions.takeaway: NSAIDs: with food, no alcohol, no doubling up, and watch the gut and kidneys.
questions.hintContent: Recall NSAID adverse effects on the GI tract, kidneys, and cardiovascular system.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each option as true or false. Watch for options that sound helpful but add to GI or renal risk.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with systemic lupus erythematosus has taken prednisone 20 mg daily for 6 months. Which findings should the nurse monitor for as adverse effects of long-term therapy? Select all that apply.
options: Elevated blood glucose
Infection with a less obvious fever and redness
Decreased bone density
Serum potassium of 3.1 mEq/L
Weight loss with a thin, drawn face
Hypoglycemia on waking
optionRationales: Correct. Glucocorticoids cause hyperglycemia.
Correct. Immunosuppression increases infection risk and masks the classic signs of inflammation.
Correct. Long-term use causes osteoporosis.
Correct. The mineralocorticoid effect causes potassium loss (hypokalemia).
Steroids cause weight gain and a round 'moon face', not weight loss.
Steroids raise, not lower, blood glucose (hypoglycemia is a risk of abrupt withdrawal, not of ongoing therapy).
questions.rationale: Long-term corticosteroid therapy causes predictable Cushingoid effects: hyperglycemia, infection risk with masked signs, osteoporosis, hypokalemia, fluid retention and hypertension, weight gain, GI ulcers, and mood changes.
questions.takeaway: Steroids: sugar up, potassium down, bones thin, infection hidden.
questions.hintContent: Recall the Cushingoid effects of long-term glucocorticoid therapy on glucose, electrolytes, bone, and immunity.
questions.hintStrategy: Check the direction of each change (up or down). Several distractors state the opposite of the true effect.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
questions.stem: A client has an inflamed, healing surgical wound. Which interventions promote tissue repair? Select all that apply.
options: Encourage lean protein at each meal
Encourage foods rich in vitamin C such as citrus and peppers
Maintain adequate oral fluid intake
Restrict protein to reduce the workload on the kidneys
Keep the client on bedrest with no position changes to protect the incision
Apply heat to the fresh incision in the first 24 hours to reduce swelling
optionRationales: Correct. Protein supplies amino acids for new tissue and collagen.
Correct. Vitamin C is required for collagen synthesis.
Correct. Hydration supports perfusion and the delivery of nutrients and WBCs to the wound.
Protein restriction impairs healing unless there is a specific renal indication.
Immobility impairs circulation and increases complications. Reposition and mobilize as allowed.
Heat causes vasodilation and more swelling in the acute phase. Cold is used early.
questions.rationale: The reparative phase needs protein, calories, vitamin C, vitamin A, zinc, and fluids. Adequate circulation, supported by mobility and positioning, delivers these building blocks to the wound.
questions.takeaway: Protein plus vitamin C plus fluids build new tissue.
questions.hintContent: Recall the nutrients and conditions needed to build collagen and new tissue.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for the options that support circulation and nutrition, and rule out any that restrict or delay healing.
