questions.stem: The nurse is counseling a client about reducing chronic inflammation. Which are modifiable risk factors? Select all that apply.
options: Cigarette smoking
Obesity
Family history of rheumatoid arthritis
A diet high in fast food and sugar
Advancing age
A personal history of psoriasis
optionRationales: Correct. Smoking promotes systemic inflammation and can be stopped.
Correct. Adipose tissue releases inflammatory cytokines, and weight can be modified.
Family history and genetics are nonmodifiable.
Correct. The Western diet is pro-inflammatory and can be changed.
Age is nonmodifiable.
A diagnosis of a chronic inflammatory disease is nonmodifiable, although it can be managed.
questions.rationale: Modifiable factors include smoking, weight, diet, physical activity, and control of hypertension and diabetes. Genetics, age, family history, and existing chronic inflammatory diseases cannot be changed but help identify clients who need screening.
questions.takeaway: You can change your habits, not your genes or your age.
questions.hintContent: Remember the difference between modifiable and nonmodifiable risk factors.
questions.hintStrategy: For each option, ask: could the client change this through behavior?

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A hospitalized client has just received the first dose of IM epinephrine for anaphylaxis. BP is 86/50 mm Hg and SpO₂ is 91%. Which additional actions should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
options: Apply high-flow oxygen
Establish large-bore IV access and give an isotonic fluid bolus as prescribed
Place the client on continuous cardiac and SpO₂ monitoring
Help the client walk to the bathroom to empty the bladder
Wait at least 1 hour before giving any repeat dose of epinephrine
Replace further epinephrine with oral diphenhydramine once the BP rises
optionRationales: Correct. Hypoxemia requires supplemental oxygen.
Correct. Capillary leak and vasodilation cause relative hypovolemia, which is treated with crystalloid.
Correct. Epinephrine and shock both raise the risk of dysrhythmias.
Standing or walking during anaphylactic shock can cause sudden cardiovascular collapse.
IM epinephrine may be repeated every 5–15 minutes if symptoms persist; waiting an hour delays life-saving treatment.
Antihistamines are adjuncts only and do not replace epinephrine for ongoing airway or circulatory symptoms.
questions.rationale: After epinephrine, supportive care includes oxygen, IV fluids, recumbent positioning, and continuous monitoring. Epinephrine is repeated every 5–15 minutes if there is no improvement, the client stays recumbent, and antihistamines and steroids are only secondary.
questions.takeaway: After epinephrine: O₂, fluids, monitor, stay flat, repeat epinephrine as needed.
questions.hintContent: Think about what else the client needs while epinephrine takes effect: oxygenation, volume, monitoring, and repeat doses.
questions.hintStrategy: Treat each option as true or false for a client who is still in shock. Ask whether it supports oxygenation, perfusion, and ongoing treatment.

questions.clientNeed: Health Promotion and Maintenance
questions.stem: The nurse is explaining why infants and young children are more vulnerable to complications of inflammation. Which factors should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
options: A relatively large tongue and narrow trachea
Immature kidneys that are less able to regulate fluid balance
Fluid losses that are more significant because total body fluid volume is smaller
More numerous and larger alveoli with greater elastic recoil
Stronger anti-inflammatory control than adults
More pro-inflammatory mediators with less ability to dampen inflammation
optionRationales: Correct. Airway edema obstructs a small airway quickly.
Correct. Immature renal function makes fluid and electrolyte balance fragile.
Correct. Small losses from fever, vomiting, or exudate are proportionally large.
Children have fewer and smaller alveoli and less elastic recoil, which increases the risk of collapse.
This is the reverse of the true difference: children have weaker, not stronger, anti-inflammatory control.
Correct. Children have more pro-inflammatory mediators and less anti-inflammatory ability, so the response can escalate.
questions.rationale: Differences in the airway, lungs, kidneys, fluid volume, and immune regulation make children more vulnerable to the effects of inflammation.
questions.takeaway: Small airway, small fluid reserves, immature kidneys, and a less-controlled inflammatory response.
questions.hintContent: Compare pediatric and adult airway, lung, kidney, fluid, and immune differences.
questions.hintStrategy: Some options state the reverse of the true pediatric difference. Read carefully for 'more' vs. 'fewer' and 'stronger' vs. 'weaker'.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client who took amoxicillin 2 years ago without problems develops anaphylaxis 10 minutes after the first dose of a new amoxicillin prescription. The client asks why a reaction happened this time. To prepare the explanation, place the events in the order in which they occurred.
options: The first exposure led the immune system to make amoxicillin-specific IgE antibodies
The IgE antibodies attached to mast cells in the tissues
On re-exposure, amoxicillin bound to the IgE on the sensitized mast cells
Mast cells released histamine, leukotrienes, and other mediators
Widespread vasodilation, capillary leak, and bronchoconstriction developed
questions.rationale: Anaphylaxis is an IgE-mediated (type I) hypersensitivity reaction that requires prior sensitization. The first exposure causes no symptoms but primes mast cells with allergen-specific IgE. On re-exposure, the allergen cross-links IgE on the mast cells, which degranulate and release histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and other mediators. These cause vasodilation, capillary leak, and bronchoconstriction within minutes, which is why an earlier uneventful course does not rule out an allergy.
questions.takeaway: Sensitize → IgE on mast cells → re-exposure → degranulation → vasodilation, leak, bronchospasm.
questions.hintContent: Recall why an allergic reaction usually does not occur on the first exposure and which cells release the mediators of anaphylaxis.
questions.hintStrategy: Anchor the first event (the earlier exposure) and the last event (the symptoms the client developed), then fill in the immune steps that connect them.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client with a deep forearm laceration asks the nurse what the body will do to heal it. To prepare the explanation, place the events of the inflammatory response in the order they occur.
options: Tissue injury and release of mediators from mast cells
Transient arteriolar vasoconstriction
Vasodilation with increased capillary permeability
Production of exudate at the site
Regeneration of tissue or scar formation
questions.rationale: Injury triggers mediator release. The vascular response (brief constriction, then dilation and leak) leads to exudate formation. The reparative phase then restores tissue by regeneration or scar.
questions.takeaway: Injury → constrict → dilate and leak → exudate → repair.
questions.hintContent: Recall the three stages of inflammation and what happens to the arterioles in the first seconds.
questions.hintStrategy: Anchor the first and last steps (injury, then repair) and fill in the vascular events between them.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: Place the steps of the cellular response in the order in which neutrophils reach and destroy bacteria at an inflamed site.
options: Margination: neutrophils move to the edge of the blood vessel
Adhesion: neutrophils stick to the endothelium
Emigration (diapedesis): neutrophils pass through the vessel wall
Chemotaxis: neutrophils move toward the chemical signal at the injury
Phagocytosis: neutrophils engulf and destroy the bacteria
questions.rationale: As blood flow slows, WBCs marginate and adhere to the vessel wall, squeeze out between endothelial cells, follow chemotactic signals to the site, and then phagocytize microbes and debris.
questions.takeaway: Line up, stick, squeeze out, follow the signal, eat.
questions.hintContent: Picture a neutrophil moving from the center of the bloodstream to the bacteria in the tissue.
questions.hintStrategy: Follow the physical path of the cell: in the vessel, through the wall, through the tissue, to the target.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: A client has a deep wound that cannot regenerate and will heal by scar formation. Place the events of repair in the order they occur.
options: A fibrin clot fills the wound
Granulation tissue with new capillaries forms
Fibroblasts deposit collagen
The wound contracts and edges draw together
The scar (cicatrix) matures into firm, pale, less vascular tissue
questions.rationale: Scar formation begins with a fibrin clot that serves as a scaffold. Granulation tissue grows in, fibroblasts lay down collagen, the wound contracts, and the scar remodels over months into avascular fibrous tissue.
questions.takeaway: Clot → granulation → collagen → contraction → mature scar.
questions.hintContent: Recall what granulation tissue needs as a scaffold and what fibroblasts produce.
questions.hintStrategy: Order the events from least organized (clot) to most organized (mature scar).

questions.ref: Module 10 · Inflammation · Acute vs. Chronic Inflammation
questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Physiological Adaptation
questions.stem: The nurse is caring for Client A, admitted with cellulitis of the leg, and Client B, who has long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. For each finding, indicate which client it is most consistent with.
rows: Red, painful swelling that developed over 6 hours
CBC shows neutrophilia with increased bands
The condition is an autoimmune disease
Symptoms for 3 years with progressive joint deformity
Findings expected to resolve with antibiotic therapy
optionRationales: Client A: rapid onset is the hallmark of acute inflammation.
Client A: neutrophils dominate the acute response, and a left shift points to bacterial infection.
Client B: RA is an autoimmune disease, a common cause of chronic inflammation that often develops independently of an acute episode.
Client B: long duration and deformity are chronic.
Client A: acute inflammation resolves when the cause is neutralized.
questions.rationale: Acute inflammation has a rapid onset, shows the classic signs, is neutrophil-driven, and resolves once the cause is neutralized. Chronic inflammation lasts months to years, often develops independently (for example, autoimmune disease), and can cause deformity.
questions.takeaway: Acute = fast, classic signs, resolves. Chronic = months to years, often autoimmune, damages tissue.
questions.hintContent: Recall the onset, duration, causes, and outcome of acute vs. chronic inflammation.
questions.hintStrategy: Link each row to the client it describes by looking at timing, cause, and whether the process resolves.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse gives a client a tetanus, diphtheria, and acellular pertussis (Tdap) vaccine IM in the left deltoid and reviews what the client may experience. For each finding, indicate whether it is an expected response or an unexpected response that requires follow-up.
rows: Redness and 2 cm of firm swelling at the injection site the next day
Soreness in the deltoid when the client lifts the arm
Hives, wheezing, and throat tightness 10 minutes after the injection
Temperature 37.8 °C (100.0 °F) and mild fatigue the evening of the injection
Increasing pain and redness on day 4 with a fluctuant area draining pus
optionRationales: Expected: a local inflammatory response (redness and swelling from vasodilation and capillary leak) is common at the injection site for 1–3 days.
Expected: pain and temporary loss of function at the site are cardinal signs of local inflammation.
Unexpected: hives, wheezing, and throat tightness within minutes of the injection indicate anaphylaxis and require epinephrine.
Expected: mild, short-lived systemic effects such as low-grade fever and fatigue reflect cytokine release and resolve within a day or two.
Unexpected: local signs that worsen after several days with a fluctuant, draining area suggest an injection-site abscess (infection), not an expected response.
questions.rationale: Vaccines deliberately trigger a small inflammatory response. Local redness, swelling, soreness, and a brief low-grade fever are expected and are managed with cool compresses and an antipyretic if needed. A reaction within minutes that involves the skin and airway is anaphylaxis, and local signs that worsen after several days with purulent drainage suggest infection; both require follow-up.
questions.takeaway: Mild local signs and low-grade fever after a vaccine are expected; rapid multisystem signs or a worsening, draining site are not.
questions.hintContent: Recall the local and mild systemic signs of an expected inflammatory response, and how timing and course help separate expected from dangerous findings.
questions.hintStrategy: For each row, look at when the finding appears and whether it is getting better or worse over time.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies
questions.stem: A client with ulcerative colitis will be discharged on a 6-week course of prednisone 40 mg daily followed by a taper. For each item in the teaching plan, indicate whether it is indicated or contraindicated.
rows: Take the dose in the morning with food
Check blood glucose if symptoms of high blood sugar develop
Stop the medication right away if you gain weight
Report a sore throat or cough even if you have no fever
Take a double dose the next day if a dose is missed
optionRationales: Indicated: morning dosing mimics the cortisol rhythm, and food reduces GI irritation.
Indicated: steroids cause hyperglycemia.
Contraindicated: abrupt discontinuation risks adrenal crisis. Weight gain is reported, not self-managed by stopping.
Indicated: steroids mask fever and inflammation, so subtle signs of infection matter.
Contraindicated: doubling doses is unsafe. The client should follow the provider's instructions for a missed dose and keep the schedule steady.
questions.rationale: Steroid teaching covers morning dosing with food, glucose monitoring, reporting infection early (signs are masked), keeping a steady schedule, and never stopping abruptly. The dose must be tapered.
questions.takeaway: Steroids: morning, with food, watch glucose, report infection early, never stop abruptly.
questions.hintContent: Recall steroid timing, glucose effects, infection masking, and withdrawal risk.
questions.hintStrategy: Look for statements that would cause harm if the client followed them.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: The nurse reviews laboratory results for a 45-year-old man admitted with an infected foot wound. For each result, indicate whether it suggests inflammation or infection, or is within normal limits.
optionRationales: Elevated: the normal ESR for men is about 0–15 mm/hr.
Elevated: CRP is normally below about 1.0 mg/dL.
Normal: the WBC range is about 5,000–10,000/mm³.
Elevated: bands above 10% indicate a left shift.
questions.rationale: ESR and CRP are nonspecific markers that rise with active inflammation, and CRP is useful for monitoring response to treatment. The total WBC count can be normal while the differential still shows a left shift.
questions.takeaway: A normal WBC does not rule out infection. Check the differential, ESR, and CRP.
questions.hintContent: Review normal ranges for ESR (by sex), CRP, total WBC, and bands.
questions.hintStrategy: Compare each value with its normal range. A normal total count does not make the whole panel normal.

questions.stem: A client stung by a wasp 10 minutes ago has lip swelling, wheezing, generalized hives, and BP 78/44 mm Hg. Complete the sentence.
questions.template: The client is most likely experiencing {0}, as evidenced by {1}. The priority medication is {2}, given {3}.

options: a local inflammatory reaction
anaphylaxis
a vasovagal episode
an asthma exacerbation
the hives alone
airway, skin, and cardiovascular involvement after exposure
the time of day the sting occurred
the location of the sting
diphenhydramine
methylprednisolone
epinephrine
albuterol
IM into the mid-anterolateral thigh
subcutaneously into the abdomen
orally with water
IM into the dorsogluteal site

questions.rationale: Rapid onset of airway, respiratory, skin, and cardiovascular symptoms after an allergen exposure is anaphylaxis. Epinephrine IM into the vastus lateralis gives the fastest, most reliable absorption and treats airway edema, bronchospasm, and hypotension.
questions.takeaway: Multisystem reaction after exposure → epinephrine IM in the thigh.
questions.hintContent: Recall the definition of anaphylaxis (multiple systems after an exposure) and the preferred route and site for the first-line drug.
questions.hintStrategy: Fill the blanks in order. Your answer to the first blank should shape the rest.

questions.stem: A 38-year-old client with seasonal allergies and a family history of thyroid disease attends a health-promotion visit. Complete the sentence.
questions.template: The nurse teaches that the best way to prevent the client's allergic inflammation is {0}. The most important measure to prevent infection-related inflammation is {1}, and screening for Hashimoto thyroiditis is done with {2}.

options: taking an antibiotic during allergy season
avoiding triggers such as dust, pollen, and animal dander
eating a high-fat, low-fiber diet
limiting daily physical activity
wearing a mask at all times
taking daily vitamin C supplements
hand hygiene
avoiding all raw foods
a thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) test
an erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR)
allergy skin testing
a white blood cell count

questions.rationale: Prevention of inflammation means avoiding triggers: allergens such as dust, pollen, and animal dander for allergies. Hand hygiene is the key to preventing infection. Screening named in the course includes allergy skin testing to identify allergens and a TSH test to detect Hashimoto thyroiditis. Antibiotics do not prevent allergies, and a high-fat, low-fiber diet and inactivity increase inflammation.
questions.takeaway: Prevention = avoid triggers + hand hygiene; screen with skin testing (allergens) and TSH (Hashimoto).
questions.hintContent: Recall the health-promotion strategies for inflammation: prevention, modifiable risk factors, and screening tests.
questions.hintStrategy: Match each blank to a different part of health promotion: preventing allergy, preventing infection, and screening.

questions.clientNeed: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
questions.stem: A client with pneumonia has T 38.7 °C (101.7 °F), HR 112, RR 24, and WBC 17,200/mm³ with 15% bands. Complete the sentence.
questions.template: The client has {0} of the systemic signs of inflammation. The elevated band count is called {1}, and the nurse should next {2}.

options: one
two
all four
none
a left shift
a right shift
eosinophilia
lymphocytosis
notify the provider promptly of the systemic findings
document the findings and reassess in 8 hours
apply ice packs to reduce the fever
restrict oral fluids

questions.rationale: Temperature above 38.5 °C, HR above 90, RR above 20, and WBC above 12,000 with increased bands are all four systemic signs of inflammation listed in the course. An increase in immature neutrophils (bands) is a left shift and suggests acute bacterial infection. Systemic findings mean the process is no longer local, so the nurse reports them promptly rather than waiting.
questions.takeaway: Fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, and leukocytosis with bands = systemic inflammation; report promptly.
questions.hintContent: Review the systemic signs of inflammation (temperature, HR, RR, WBC) and what an increase in bands is called.
questions.hintStrategy: Count the signs one at a time against the cutoffs before choosing the next action.
